q1: SELECT T.SEMESTER, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM DEPARTMENT AS D INNER JOIN TEACHES AS T ON (D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4) INNER JOIN COURSE AS C ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY T.SEMESTER HAVING AVG(C.CREDITS) > 2 AND COUNT(D.BUILDING) = 2
q2: SELECT T.SEMESTER, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM DEPARTMENT AS D INNER JOIN TEACHES AS T ON (D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4) INNER JOIN COURSE AS C ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY T.SEMESTER HAVING AVG(C.CREDITS) > 2 AND COUNT(D.BUILDING) >= 2

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because they differ in the HAVING clause. Q1 uses COUNT(D.BUILDING) = 2, while Q2 uses COUNT(D.BUILDING) >= 2. This means Q2 could return results for groups with more than 2 rows, whereas Q1 restricts to exactly 2 rows.
counterexample_dsp: A test database where one semester group has exactly 2 rows (matching Q1) but not Q2's condition, and another semester group has 3 rows (matching Q2 but not Q1).
